It is said that the problem with self-analysis is the protective blindness to the countertransference. But, in Individualizing Gender and Sexuality, Nancy Chodorow treats us to her self-analytic double vision: A retrospective view about how her contributions as a key feminist theorist developed, from her early writings in the 1970s until now, as well as a refreshing appraisal of reasons why she has revised some of her earlier formulations. Her essays brim with incisive, wry, and at times humorous insights, as well as changes of heart. She ascribes the latter mostly to the dual experiences of becoming a mother and entering psychoanalytic training. Chodorow argues against the dogmatic assumptions about gendered identity and sexual experience that have crept into past psychoanalytic theory and practice. She depicts multiple influences that shape complex, unique, and often conflicted layers of sexual meanings in relation to the subjective sense of self. The chapters, based on previously presented papers, address cultural, Relational, and developmental contributions to such individuality.

Chodorow also portrays how the mutability of sexual and gendered experience reflects its historical and relational context while the development of a viable sense of self is being formed. The challenge and/or celebration of integrating such disparate aspects of self have had nuanced literary dramatizations as well. For example, the spirited, cross-dressing, sex-changing Orlando (Woolf, 1928) begins life as a young nobleman in 16th-century England and moves through numerous historical and geographical worlds to become a woman writer in the 1920s. Orlando transcends both age and gender to have it all, not without his/her share of both joys and distress in each gendered position, within its culture, in which she finds him-/herself.

Lou's book—most of his patients addressed him as Lou—is filled with his patients' reactions to their treatment. A distinguished psychoanalyst, he aims this book at people considering psychological treatment, and provides commentaries from many of the patients (in their own words) he has helped or not helped in their analytic work together. He cites only three other books in the past several decades with comparable detailed descriptions by patients of their analytic treatment.1

The tone and thesis are established in the first paragraph of the prologue, written by a former patient named Elizabeth. She comments “that Not Knowing” was okay” (p. ix). It is unlikely that Elizabeth is aware of Jonathan Lear's description of the affliction widespread among psychoanalysts that he termed “Knowingness,” i.e., knowing all one needs to know about psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic treatment. Lou either has a very strong constitution or had the benefit of an effective vaccination, because he seems immune to this common analytic ailment, and that is clear to his appreciative patients. Perhaps it is an expression of analysts' “Knowingness” that they fail to consider, as Lou does, that they may have a good deal to learn from their patients' views. His freedom from this affliction enables him to demonstrate how much can be learned from patients' views.

One important theme of the book is the patient's need to feel cared about, indeed, deeply cared about, by the therapist. Several patients cited their conviction that Lou really liked them, and the role that feeling played in their coming to like themselves. Lou wrote that it is “impossible to work at a deep emotional level with people over long periods without developing real affection for them” (p. 113). In one attuned expression of affection, he sent a patient a couple of CDs after learning she shared his enjoyment of the same music. As another patient, a young man who had reported having had too much to drink the previous night, left the session, Lou said, gently, “And don't drink too much tonight” (p. 43).

Interpersonal and Relational psychoanalysts are comfortable approaching categories of race and gender as socially constructed—and as fertile ground for the exploration and co-construction of new meanings in the process of psychotherapy. Using myself as an example, I focus on a particular aspect of gender, ethnicity, and race, and how their meanings are sometimes forged in a family environment where the sense of identity is part and parcel of ongoing social trauma, and where survival means staying within the invisible boundaries set by the anxiety-laden compromises of previous generations. Of central concern is the role of witness and the conflicts and complexities that come with it.

Ruth Livingston

Ruth Livingston  

WE ARE GREATLY HONORED to be the new Editors-in-Chief of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, proud to take the reins and carry forth the legacy of scholarly inquiry, collaboration, and inclusiveness the journal has championed since its launch in 1964. We thank founders Rose Spiegel and Max Deutscher, and the editors who followed—Arthur Feiner, Jay Greenberg, Donnel Stern, Philip Bromberg, and, most recently, Mark Blechner—for steering Contemporary Psychoanalysis into the 21st century. Along the way, our predecessors published the works of seminal thinkers in Interpersonal and Relational psychoanalysis as well as influential contributions from other schools and disciplines. We intend to follow their lead.

We are excited about the challenges we face in this increasingly fastpaced, technologically, culturally, and sociologically bewildering moment —when the world is smaller than ever before; when attention spans are reduced to texts and tweets; when the printed word itself seems to be disappearing; when psychoanalysis is routinely dismissed as anachronistic, impractical, and inefficient; and when the profession has been marginalized by many mental health professionals and laypersons alike.

Being on the margins (Stepansky, 2009), however, does not preclude psychoanalysis from playing a vital and transformative role in individuals' lives and in the life of our times. It is easy to forget that when a person experiences and undergoes profound change—as often happens in psychoanalytic therapy—the lives of many others, including children, are often transformed as well, which greatly multiplies the effect of our work. In short, we have an impact on far more people than we actually treat. Moreover, psychoanalysis, like the U.S. Constitution and Bill of Rights, safeguards principles and values (such as confidentiality, individuality, genuineness, and interiority) that are—and perhaps always will be—un-der threat. The true impact of psychoanalysis on today's culture, however, may only be discernible in hindsight, many years from now.

Some of the leading 20th-century philosophical inheritors of Enlightenment thought turned to psychoanalysis as a crucial part of their analysis of the social and individual dynamics of domination and submission. In explaining the ways in which individual pathologies intersect with authoritarian political ideologies and social hatreds, the “Frankfurt School” theorists developed a psychoanalytically informed social theory. They understood that strivings for freedom could not be accomplished only by political revolution. They also had to be accompanied by a transformed internal psychic life that could embrace freedom as essential to psychic and social health. These thinkers held that psychoanalysis was necessary to actualize freedom based on critical subjective agency as concrete realities of daily life. Otherwise, social theory remains detached from individual human experience. This article argues for the relevance and necessity of psychoanalysis for social change. It includes a clinical vignette that illustrates the ways in which individual pathologies intersect with, sustain, and reproduce social intolerance and prejudice.

The British analyst Marion Milner begins her prescient book, On Not Being Able to Paint (1957), by wondering if her “preconceived ideas about beauty in drawing might have a limiting effect on one's freedom of expression.” When self-conscious cogitation fails her, Milner considers that “beauty might be like happiness, something which a too direct striving after destroys” (p. 5). An entire volume later, she concludes that painting indeed requires “A-never-before-known wholeness” involving “thought and sensation and feeling and action,” the result being “not a lessening of the objective powers but a strengthening, once the needs of their opposite have been given recognition … this different kind of sense of self that grew out of creative concentration had bearings upon one's relation to the whole mass of other selves that one was in contact with” (p. 142).

Only years later, however, as a result of the seminal writings of Philip Bromberg (1998, 2006), has the felicitous clatter of the consulting room been recognized as central to the analytic process and therapeutic action. It is not that Bromberg's current volume, The Shadow of the Tsunami and the Growth of the Relational Mind, lacks careful thought and scholarship, drawing as it does from the likes of Harry Stack Sullivan, Emily Dickenson, D. W. Winnicott, Edgar Levenson, Robert Burns, and research in neuroscience (hence the laudatory foreword written by the neuropsychoanalyst Allen Schore). Yet, as Milner suggests, received wisdom is not always relevant, or not exclusively so.

Goldberg, virtually unique among psychoanalysts, asserts that the subject of psychoanalytic failure, largely ignored by its practitioners and academics, is a subject of critical significance to psychoanalysis. Psychoanalytic Electronic Publishing (PEP), covering thousands of references, reveals only four references to “psychoanalytic failure” whereas “psychoanalytic theory” garners 648 references. How can psychoanalytic success be defined without the counterdefinition of psychoanalytic failure? (A book edited by J. Reppen and M. A. Schulman [2002] presented a large number of varied, illuminating clinical examples of analytic failures.)

Goldberg notes, “A surprisingly large number of cases in psychoanalysis seem to fit into this category (i.e., “the patient just quit”) (p. 206). He adds, “The tendency to ignore or deny the likelihood of failure is the greatest boon to its eventual emergence” (p. 211). Because Goldberg refers to both “therapists” and “analysts,” I will enlarge the discussion by utilizing observations about psychotherapy as well as observations about psychoanalysis, because research data about psychotherapy is not only more abundant but necessary to enhance our perspective and understanding of its problems. I put aside the unresolved controversies over whether psychotherapy and psychoanalysis are qualitatively different.

Every life is a story. We say a person has a life story because we recognize that imagination, a kind of dreaming, is crucial to living. We must imagine ourselves in order to utilize, or to brook, the impact of circumstance and, most especially, influence. As much as we are pushed and prodded by material reality, we are shaped by dreams. Where a life

590

is concerned, what happened matters, but it is never the whole story. In the precincts of biography, inventory is no substitute for imagination. Epistemologically speaking, facts may bear little relation to the truth. The heart of biography is essentially paradoxical: a subject must be dreamed awake; he must be imagined to be real. An inventory of a life, then, must by definition incorporate invention, not in the sense of fabricating but in the sense of imagining, of wondering. How we organize and reconvene experience—how we imagine ourselves consequent to it—is how we become the persons we are, how we have a story to begin with.

In Sullivan Revisited: Life and Work, Marco Conci has given us an exhaustive, at times astonishing, compendium of information pertaining to Harry Stack Sullivan's formidable contributions to psychoanalysis and social psychiatry. The book is a richly detailed and contextualized survey of Sullivan's influence and influences. Much of this detail is important and adds to our understanding of Sullivan's thinking and the intellectual milieu in which it developed. Though Sullivan Revisited is not, strictly speaking, a biography, its reach includes a concern with the impact Sullivan's experience had on the development of his Interpersonal theory and technique as well as some effort to trace that effect. But although Conci has voluminously researched Sullivan, he has not captured him, because, I think, he has not fully imagined him. In particular, he has not allowed a depth appreciation of the crucial impact Sullivan's subjective experiences had on the establishment and elaboration of his most important ideas.

By taking a social psychological approach, this article seeks to offer an alternative perspective to the traditional psychoanalytic studies of Freud and Ferenczi's close personal and professional relationship, and the rift that occurred in the early 1930s. It is suggested that the socially constructed, divergent roles that these two men fulfilled in the psychoanalysis movement deeply influenced the dynamics of their relationship. It is further proposed that the ever-present, conflicted political interdependence that characterized Freud's and Ferenczi's home countries (Austria and Hungary, respectively) may have affected them differently, and contributed to their divergent attitudes towards power and other issues relevant to the development of psychoanalytic theory and technique, as well as how they related to one another personally.

Danielle Knafo's impressive book deals with 10 female artists—most with established reputations—whose “daringly subversive” self-representational works form a trajectory of female gender representation in the 20th century. In Her Own Image is infused with the

121

psychological lives of these artists, for the artists are both subject and object of their art. The richness of the book's psychoanalytic, historical, and feminist inquiry is suggested by the chapter headings, e.g., “Käthe Kollwitz: The Dead Mother” and “Claude Cahun: The Third Sex.” We move from the social realism of Kollwitz (1867-1945) through the idiosyncratic surrealism of Cahun (1894-1954) and Frida Kahlo (1907-1954) to Charlotte Salomon's (1917-1942) intermedia narrative of trauma, a cross between theater and art. Her work can be thought of as a kind of prelude to the later performance art, documented in photographs, of Ana Mendieta (1945-1984), Adrian Piper (b. 1948), Cindy Sherman (b. 1954), Carolee Schneeman (b. 1947), Hannah Wilke (1940-1993), and Orlan (b. 1947). The range is breathtaking; the biographical information is comprehensive; the writing is incisive. Taken together, the book offers an overview of the ideas that informed 20th-century art in general and 20th-century women's art in particular.

Knafo is a clinical psychologist, psychoanalyst, art critic, feminist, and professor. A historical, feminist critique informs her thinking. She cites Linda Nochlin, Whitney Chadwick, Lucy Lippard, Griselda Pollock, and many other writers whose ideas helped her historicize women and art (p. 18). “In Her Own Image,” she writes, “extends the dialogue between art history and feminism, while developing a psychoanalytic examination of women's self-representation” (p. 18). Knafo also joins the collective efforts of others who work in the “intersection of feminism, psychoanalysis, and other disciplines,” e.g., Dorothy Dinnerstein, Nancy Chodorow, Jessica Benjamin, Muriel Dimen, and Adrienne Harris. She notes the tension between “theoretical gender” (as constructed in the academy) and the “psychological gender of lived experience explicated in the clinic” (p. 18), while believing the gap between the two can be traversed. In this work, artists' “psychological” lives and self-representations are not simply grist for a parochial theoretical mill, nor fodder for the narcissism of small differences; they are contained in—and handled as—sensitizing theories that speak to the psychological and art act simultaneously. Each can inform and enhance the other. Her deft curating of the aesthetic, emotional, and social historical context of these lives and works is a compelling interdisciplinary contribution to understanding a major aspect of 20th-century history: woman's self-representation.

Donnell Stern is a central figure in American psychoanalysis. More than a major American contributor to international psychoanalysis, he is a key voice in what might arguably be viewed as an American psychoanalytic tradition that stretches back to Harry Stack Sullivan, a literature with insights into psychopathology and analytic process that is equally important, and in some ways similar, to those found in the writings of D. W. Winnicott and Wilfred Bion. The subtitle of his new book, Partners in Thought, summarizes the foci of his life's work: unformulated experience, dissociation, and enactment.

Because a near-cult formed in response to Bion's notions of beta and alpha elements (i.e., his theory of unmentalized versus more mindful thinking), it is easy to overlook that awareness of this distinction goes back to Freud and Sullivan. In 1915, Freud (1917/1957) wrote: “The conscious presentation comprises the presentation of the thing plus the presentation of the word belonging to it, while the unconscious presentation is the presentation of the thing alone” (p. 201). Sullivan (1954), who is Stern's primary source, conceptualized a “not-me” state of being (or what we now call a “self-state”) in which the person wards off alpha-ing, articulating, or formulating experiences that are literally inconceivable and unthinkable without destruction of the self. Philip Bromberg also resurrected and elaborated Sullivan's notion and his and Stern's work forms another cornerstone of the American literature, which, I argue, runs equal and parallel to the literature created by Winnicott and Bion.

Toward an emancipatory psychoanalysis, a collection of articles by Bernard Brandchaft, does a good job depicting the evolution of his thinking about accommodative tendencies and their treatment. Compiled by Brandchaft with coeditors Shelley Doctors and Dorienne Sorter, this collection includes chronologically organized articles accompanied by informative commentaries that carefully outline the points in each article and their contribution to Brandchaft's evolving narrative. Doctors and Sorter have made a significant contribution to the larger psychoanalytic community by initiating and organizing this collection. Reading the articles and the commentaries, one is impressed by the ubiquity of accommodative tendencies in development and psychopathology, and Brandchaft's ideas about how to conduct psychoanalysis with accommodative patients are instructive.

In his signature article, “To Free the Spirit from its Cell” (Brandchaft, 1993), Brandchaft presents two patients, Patrick and Marco, who vacillate inexplicably between expansive states related to authentic self-expression to more depressed states reflecting their parents' lifelong critical view of them. Brandchaft relates this vacillation to the power of their accommodative tendencies: their tendency to regard themselves and their experience according to their parents' critical and demanding perspectives.

In Brandchaft's view, patients such as Marco and Patrick grow up defining themselves in what he refers as an “accommodative” way—accommodating, that is, to their parent's view—in order to develop and sustain a positive tie with parents who have related to them as extensions or projections of their own subjectivity. Not experiencing recognition and affirmation for their own authentic perspective, these patients did not develop their own unique perspective. Instead, they adapted to the self-centered reflections they received from their caregivers.

The biblical narrative of the Binding of Isaac conveys conflicting messages. On the one hand, it demands a readiness to sacrifice one's beloved at God's command. On the other hand, the narrative's conclusion cancels the sacrifice of the son and ordains his replacement with an animal, a ram. This article argues that the ancient rabbis of the Midrash, in the first centuries of the Common Era, perceived this ambiguity as an inherent tension between the religious demand for the believer's willingness to sacrifice his dearest, and even life itself, and the danger of a perverted overenthusiasm to sacrifice and be sacrificed. This article further suggests that classical psychoanalytic interpretations of the biblical story, as well as proposed interpretations from the perspectives of self psychology and Interpersonal and Relational psychoanalysis, can contribute to an understanding of this tension. Murderous and masochistic Oedipal wishes may contribute to a willingness to engage in child sacrifice and martyrdom, and deeply rooted desires to express and actualize the nuclear self and to attain a close relationship with idealized entities are described as competing and struggling forces in this heroic and complicated narrative. Contemporary ramifications of this interpretation are discussed.

The psychological and emotional growth of the analyst is easily overlooked or taken for granted, and its impact has been largely ignored theoretically. But, it is woven into the treatment in unseen and powerful ways, often emerging in the heat of the interaction, as the analyst struggles with the threats and challenges of relating to the patient. In this article, I argue that the analyst's growth pulls the patient toward a similar growth. I have called that pull “beckoning.” It is an aspect of mutual regulation and intersubjective life wherein one person brings another to a more enriched place by standing in it him- or herself. The analyst's beckoning, often unconscious and inadvertent, is an element in the unwinding of enactments, which, in turn, leads to the coconstruction of a more mature connection.

Recently, a number of people of Chinese descent (first-generation Americans and recent immigrants) have contacted me for psychotherapy. Many complain that they do not know who they are or that they are confused about their professional and personal goals. My attempt to understand their complaints has led me in two directions, each of which is briefly described in this article. First, I have had to learn something about the trauma experienced by some of their parents during the Cultural Revolution and the effects it had on them. In a style of relating I call “imparted connoisseurship,” one person acting as a hyperdiscriminating “master” inducts another in the role of eager “disciple” into a preoccupation with the finer points of a mutually compelling interest or endeavor. In its unhealthy version, instead of enriching and strengthening the other, this form of relating coercively co-opts the psyche of the disciple. It generates self-critical shame in the disciple, or evokes a wafer-thin feeling of superiority that defends against a heightened unconscious sense of personal insufficiency and self-contempt. The damaging version of imparted connoisseurship belongs within the set of intrapsychic and interpersonal phenomena I call “micro-trauma,” an insidious if subtle psychic bruising that gradually erodes one's sense of wellbeing, efficacy, and/or self-worth. In this article, I explore destructive connoisseurship as it plays out in various configurations-between two peers, mentor and protégé, parent and child, analytic supervisor and supervisee, and analyst and patient.

Immigrant psychology and mental health have become of interest to academics, mental health professionals, and governments, which is not surprising because issues of immigration have important social, political, economic, and psychological dimensions. Boulanger (2004) notes that although psychoanalysis was created and dominated for a long time by immigrants, the number of psychoanalytic authors addressing immigration remains small, and the contributions themselves are relatively recent. I contend that unformulated (Stern, 1997) dissociative experiences of temporo-spatial discontinuity (Akhtar, 1999) lie at the heart of the immigrant's experience. Sometimes these experiences find expression in dreams, or are revealed in unexpected feelings and thoughts triggered by an event that concretely represents discontinuity. I also identify some variations, which I label as the awareness surge, the perplexing clarity, and the two-point existence.

Culture and history play a constitutive role in human psychology and their impact is both conscious and unconscious. This article addresses the unconscious dimension of culture and history in human experience by examining Mark Freeman's notion of the narrative unconscious. Drawing on the themes of narrative, memory, culture, and hermeneutics, I provide a context for understanding the narrative unconscious and point to parallels with contemporary psychoanalysis. The European Shoah affected the lives of the majority of the psychoanalysts who founded and shaped the new “science.” How one discerns the impact of such an upheaval on theoretical and clinical material, however, becomes a epistemological problem that is the subject of this article. In keeping with the Zeitgeist of most of the 20th century, professional writing from the period tends to read as transcendent truth immune to context, so that the influence of catastrophe remains, at best, implicit. Although deconstructing texts proves useful at certain junctures, these interpretations are highly subjective, and threaten to degenerate into armchair psychoanalyses that presume and, worse, pathologize. Thus, I turn to interviews conducted with analysts who lived during the period, or who have studied the Shoah. These dialogues explore how the Nazi scourge transformed a theoretical and clinical tradition. But here the plot thickens, for if a period of ineffable trauma inclines towards enactment rather than mentalization, to talk about it is to act it out. Thus, my method is at times nearly indistinguishable from its goal. If the interviews in this article convey factual information, they also enact the very content under discussion. Put differently, the words on the page, particularly those between interviewees and myself, are informative, but in part as “transforms,” as Edgar Levenson (1972) would put it, of what has been recorded as commentary. And yet these narratives echo the story of a movement that changed, and was changed by history.

The development of psychoanalytic technique can be traced in part to the dialogues between Sigmund Freud and Sándor Ferenczi, dialogues that took place in the context of psychoanalysis's encounter with poverty and destitution in the wake of World War I. These dialogues, which served as precursors to contemporary, especially Relational, psychoanalysis, also inspired Freud's call for greater psychoanalytic engagement with the poorest and most vulnerable. This inspired the early psychoanalysts to “sharpen in all directions the sense of social justice” by engaging in political activism, experimenting with clinical technique, and by promoting short-term, more affordable treatments. The relevance of this history for clinical work with diverse populations will be discussed, and aspects of contemporary psychoanalysis (countertransference, enactment, new relational experience) will be understood in light of Freud and Ferenczi's responsiveness to the underprivileged.

In this article, I offer a concept of therapeutic action that I call “the flow of enactive engagement.” I advance the idea that this flow of enactive engagement is the fulcrum of a contemporary psychoanalytic treatment, just as free association was once to classical psychoanalysis. Analyst and analysand live within the field of the treatment that is created by the two participants but is greater than the sum of its parts. Just as Freud saw free association as the road to psychoanalytic cure and advised the analyst to not intrude on the analysand's associations, I suggest that an unobtrusive Relational analyst can allow the process of the field to emerge and tell its own story. This approach is distinguished from the traditional Relational/Interpersonal approach that sees the constant examination of the therapeutic interaction as the key to therapeutic action. I offer a brief vignette that captures the analytic benefits that accrue when the analyst allows the flow of enactive engagement to unfold.

This article discusses some of Irene Fast's notable contributions to fundamental psychoanalytic issues. Here is how she begins:

I am tired. Psychoanalysis makes me incredibly tired. I have spent a greater part of my time hating psychoanalysis. I can't read another paper. I want the whole thing to collapse. I see it teetering on the edge of its abyss, and think I'm done, it is done. And yet somehow I know that it could do nothing else—it is precarious, it has been from the beginning. What have I been hoping for? What did I expect? Apparently a whole lot. (p. 1)

Jamieson Webster, a newly minted psychoanalyst, and a teacher at Eugene Lang College and New York University, is disillusioned and disappointed. The Life and Death of Psychoanalysis is an audacious debut—Webster utilizes her dreams, memories of analytic training, and her encounters with intellectual idols to explore the nature of desire, and in so doing returns the subject of desire to the center of analytic discourse. She opens her book telling us she feels her hope has been betrayed. Already her tone is personal and confessional. Webster goes on to structure her book around three of her own dreams, not attempting to use them as illustrations—that would be pedantic and she knows it—but rather as “a provocation to thought” (p. xxiii). Blurring the line between memoir and theoretical psychoanalysis, Webster unblinkingly pursues an animating passion, a force that may reveal unconscious desire, something that may, for her at least, keep the edifice of psychoanalysis from falling down around her. The result is a new form of psychoanalytic writing, one that is not quite wholly intellectual memoir, nor strictly philosophic text, and yet is a hybrid of those forms that is able to speak of psychoanalysis from a different vantage point.

The Life and Death of Psychoanalysis may have been written at the Chelsea Hotel (at least that's my fantasy), for I can hear Leonard Cohen in the pages lamenting love and its eventual loss, crushed idealism, and how everything has a hole in it.

Ferrara (1994) estimates that 19-35% of the utterances by psychotherapists in session are variations of mm-hmm. However, there has been little discussion of this phenomenon in the literature. According to linguistics theory, mm-hmm constitutes a backchannel response to a speaker that affirms his or her right to continue to hold the floor. In psychotherapy, mm-hmm reaffirms the patient's right to an extended conversational turn and the therapist's role as listener. Because mm-hmm is unobtrusive and ambiguous, however, unconscious issues in the therapeutic relationship can be communicated through its variations. Psychotherapists should understand the function of mm-hmm in maintaining the structure of the therapeutic relationship and be aware that it can be easily enlisted in the service of unconscious communications.
